title: Week 23 · Lesson 47: Geriatric Pharmacology — Polypharmacy, Deprescribing, Falls & Medication Safety
html:
PHASE 2 · ADVANCED PHARMACOLOGY

Week 23 — Lesson 47: Geriatric Pharmacology — Polypharmacy, Deprescribing, Falls & Medication Safety

FNP-level goal: Build a medication plan around function, goals, life expectancy, kidney/liver reserve, cognition, falls, and patient priorities—not simply a longer list of disease-specific prescriptions.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain why aging, multimorbidity, and polypharmacy increase adverse-drug-event risk.
  • Perform a structured medication reconciliation that includes OTC products, supplements, duplicate therapy, and prescriber coordination.
  • Recognize medication patterns associated with falls, delirium, orthostasis, hypoglycemia, bleeding, and kidney injury.
  • Apply safe deprescribing principles without abruptly stopping medications that require tapering or specialist coordination.
  • Use patient goals and functional outcomes to guide prescribing in older adults.

Part 1 — Polypharmacy Is a Clinical Signal, Not a Number Alone

Polypharmacy means the use of multiple medications. It can be appropriate when each medication has a clear evidence-based indication, benefit, and monitoring plan. It becomes dangerous when medications are duplicated, no longer needed, interact with each other, exceed organ clearance capacity, treat a side effect caused by another drug, or no longer match the patient’s goals.

Do not ask only, “How many medications?” Ask, “What is each medication for, does it still help this patient, what harm could it cause now, and what would happen if it were reduced or stopped?” The patient’s function, cognition, falls, frailty, kidney function, prognosis, and priorities can change the answer.

Part 2 — Medication Reconciliation Is Diagnosis

A complete list includes prescriptions from every clinician, OTC pain/cold/sleep products, vitamins, herbals, topical agents, inhalers, eye drops, PRN drugs, alcohol, and substances. Ask the patient or caregiver to bring bottles or photographs. Compare the list with the actual use pattern; the chart list often differs from what is taken.

For every medication, identify indication, dose, schedule, start date, intended duration, prescriber, perceived benefit, adverse effects, kidney/liver considerations, interactions, and monitoring. This turns a “med list cleanup” into a diagnostic and safety intervention.

Part 3 — Pharmacokinetics Change With Age

Kidney function, hepatic metabolism, body composition, protein binding, and physiologic reserve can change with aging and acute illness. A medication tolerated for years may become unsafe after dehydration, weight loss, infection, new kidney injury, hospitalization, or addition of another drug.

Use current kidney function and clinical context, not a historic creatinine value alone. Review renal dosing, blood pressure, orthostatic symptoms, electrolytes, glucose, bleeding risk, and cognitive change when medication safety is in question.

Part 4 — The Prescribing Cascade

A prescribing cascade occurs when an adverse effect is mistaken for a new disease and another medication is added. Examples include medication-related edema treated with an unnecessary diuretic, drug-induced orthostasis treated as “weakness,” or anticholinergic effects interpreted as a new bladder condition.

When a new symptom appears, ask: What changed in the medication list, dose, adherence, hydration, renal function, or OTC use? A timeline can prevent a cascade before it grows into polypharmacy, falls, emergency visits, and loss of independence.

Part 5 — Falls Are Often Medication-Related

Falls are multifactorial, but medications can contribute through sedation, dizziness, slowed reaction time, vision change, hypoglycemia, orthostatic hypotension, bradycardia, weakness, or impaired balance. High-risk patterns include combinations of CNS-active medications, sedatives, opioids, benzodiazepines, anticholinergic burden, antihypertensives/diuretics in a vulnerable volume state, and glucose-lowering treatment that causes hypoglycemia.

After any fall, near-fall, new unsteadiness, or fear of falling, review the entire medication list and timing. Do not assume the answer is a mobility aid alone or automatically discontinue every blood-pressure medication; identify the patient-specific mechanism and balance benefit against harm.

Part 6 — Delirium, Cognition, and Anticholinergic Burden

New confusion in an older adult is acute medical illness until proven otherwise. Medication effects, infection, dehydration, urinary retention, constipation, hypoxia, metabolic disturbance, pain, withdrawal, and intracranial pathology are all possible contributors. A sedating or anticholinergic medication can worsen attention, memory, gait, and urinary function.

Do not prescribe an additional sedative for a suddenly confused patient before evaluating delirium. Ask about OTC sleep aids, antihistamines, bladder agents, muscle relaxants, opioids, benzodiazepines, and recently changed medications. Protect safety and arrange urgent evaluation when cognition changes abruptly.

Part 7 — Orthostasis and Blood Pressure: Treat the Patient, Not Only the Number

Older adults can experience dizziness, falls, syncope, kidney injury, or reduced function when blood pressure treatment, volume status, and autonomic reserve are not balanced. Obtain orthostatic symptoms and appropriate vital signs, assess hydration, recent illness, diuretic use, alcohol, and medication timing.

Do not react to one clinic blood-pressure value by automatically intensifying therapy in a patient reporting recurrent lightheadedness or falls. Confirm measurements, review home data when available, and individualize targets and follow-up within current guidelines and the patient’s goals.

Part 8 — Hypoglycemia Is a Geriatric Medication Emergency Pattern

Hypoglycemia can present atypically in older adults—as confusion, weakness, a fall, behavior change, diaphoresis, or syncope. Risk increases with insulin or insulin-secretagogue exposure, poor intake, acute illness, kidney dysfunction, medication errors, and changing caregiving support.

When an older adult’s intake, weight, kidney function, or goals change, re-evaluate diabetes medications and monitoring plan. Avoid treating an A1c value as more important than recurrent low glucose, falls, or inability to safely manage a complex regimen.

Part 9 — Bleeding, Kidney Injury, and OTC Harm

OTC products are common sources of hidden risk. NSAIDs, antihistamines, sleep products, cold remedies, antacids, laxatives, herbals, and duplicate acetaminophen-containing products can interact with chronic prescriptions or worsen kidney, blood-pressure, bleeding, cognitive, or fall risk.

Ask specifically rather than saying, “Any other medications?” A patient may not consider a nightly sleep aid, herbal tea, topical analgesic, or pharmacy cold product a medication. Medication reconciliation should include exact products and frequency.

Part 10 — Deprescribing Is a Planned Clinical Intervention

Deprescribing means supervised dose reduction or discontinuation of a medication when current harms, burden, or lack of benefit outweigh expected benefit. It is not abandoning care and it is not an abrupt stop order for every medication. Some medications need tapering; others require specialist coordination; still others remain essential despite advanced age.

Start with shared goals. Select one or a small number of high-priority targets, explain the rationale, make a taper/monitoring plan when appropriate, identify withdrawal or disease-recurrence symptoms, and schedule reassessment. Document who owns the plan so another prescriber does not inadvertently restart the medication.

Part 11 — Potentially Inappropriate Medication Tools Support Judgment

Tools such as the AGS Beers Criteria can identify medication classes that are often best avoided or used with caution in older adults, drug-disease interactions, drug-drug interactions, and kidney-based dose concerns. They are screening tools—not universal prohibition lists.

A medication on a cautionary list may still be appropriate for a carefully selected patient. Conversely, a medication not listed can still be harmful in a particular patient. Use these tools alongside diagnosis, evidence, patient goals, frailty, pharmacology, and shared decision-making.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: The New Fall After a “Successful” Visit

An 82-year-old with hypertension, neuropathic pain, insomnia, and anxiety reports two falls after a recent medication change. The list includes a nighttime sedative, an opioid, a gabapentinoid, a diuretic, and a new antihypertensive dose increase.

FNP reasoning: identify timing, orthostatic symptoms, renal function, alcohol/OTC use, glucose, cognition, and actual dose use. This may be a cumulative medication effect, not simply “old age.” Stabilize urgent risks and coordinate a prioritized medication review rather than adding another sedative for sleep.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: Confusion Is Not Automatically Dementia

A 76-year-old with stable mild cognitive impairment develops abrupt confusion, dry mouth, urinary retention, and unsteady gait after starting an OTC sleep product.

FNP reasoning: acute onset demands delirium assessment. The medication history and anticholinergic pattern are clinically important, but infection, metabolic disease, and other urgent causes must also be considered. Stop unsafe self-treatment only within a complete urgent evaluation plan.

Part 14 — Clinical Case: Overtreatment of Diabetes

An older adult with kidney disease and inconsistent meals has recurrent morning confusion and a recent fall. Their diabetes regimen has not changed despite reduced appetite and weight loss.

FNP reasoning: evaluate for hypoglycemia and medication accumulation. Reassess glycemic targets, regimen complexity, nutrition, caregiver support, and renal dosing. Safety and function may outweigh a highly intensive numeric target.

FNP Geriatric Pharmacology Framework

  1. Reconcile every prescription, OTC product, supplement, PRN medication, alcohol, and actual use pattern.
  2. For each drug, confirm indication, benefit, harm, interaction, dose/organ function, monitoring, and patient goal.
  3. Screen medication-related symptoms after every fall, delirium, dizziness, bleeding event, kidney injury, weight/intake change, or hospitalization.
  4. Use cautionary tools to prompt review, not to replace individualized judgment.
  5. Deprescribe deliberately: prioritize, taper when needed, monitor, document ownership, and follow up.
  6. Escalate urgently for syncope, serious fall injury, acute delirium, severe hypoglycemia, bleeding, overdose, or inability to manage medications safely.

High-Yield Summary

Polypharmacy: may be appropriate, but every medication needs a current indication and benefit-harm review.
Falls: medication combinations can cause sedation, orthostasis, hypoglycemia, and impaired balance.
New confusion: evaluate delirium and medication/OTC exposure urgently; do not label it dementia by default.
Kidney function: illness and aging can change medication exposure quickly.
Deprescribing: is supervised, patient-centered, and usually gradual—not abrupt withdrawal.
Function and goals: matter as much as disease-specific metrics in older adults.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Medication reconciliation, prescribing, tapering, renal dosing, diabetes management, fall assessment, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, FDA-approved prescribing information, local scope requirements, and the individual patient’s clinical context.
